findings.title: SQL injection in the invoice type-ahead search
findings.evidence: $term = trim($request->query('q', '')) at line 47 is interpolated directly into the statement at line 57: "and (number like '%{$term}%' or notes like '%{$term}%')". The same DB::select call binds only account_id as a positional parameter, so the sibling value on the same line proves the binding mechanism was available and not used for $term.
findings.impact: Any authenticated portal user can break out of the LIKE literal and read or modify anything the database role can reach, including other tenants' invoices, since the account_id predicate can be neutralised by the injected text.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term: "and (number like ? or notes like ?)" with ['%'.$term.'%', '%'.$term.'%'], as the account_id parameter on the same call already does.

triage.reason: no escaping, allowlist or prepared-statement layer sits between $request->query('q') and the statement; the route only carries the 'auth' middleware (routes/web.php:38)
the value is the raw q query parameter, trimmed only

findings.title: Invoice detail is fetched by id with no account scoping while its sibling handlers scope theirs
findings.evidence: show() calls Invoice::with('account')->findOrFail($id) with no tenant predicate. update() at line 101 and download() at line 113 both begin Invoice::where('account_id', $request->user()->account_id), so the asymmetry is decidable inside this one file. The Invoice model declares no global scope (app/Models/Invoice.php) and the route carries only the 'auth' middleware.
findings.impact: Any signed-in customer can read any other customer's invoice, including the eager-loaded account record, by incrementing the numeric id in /invoices/{id}.
findings.recommendation: Scope the lookup the way the sibling handlers do, or resolve the model through a policy: Invoice::where('account_id', $request->user()->account_id)->with('account')->findOrFail($id).

triage.reason: no middleware, policy or model scope injects the tenant filter; the two sibling handlers apply it by hand, which is exactly the layer a caller can forget
the route sits inside the auth group, so the data is not public by design
the record holds another customer's billing amounts, status and account relation

findings.title: Invoice update mass-assigns the whole request body through forceFill
findings.evidence: $invoice->forceFill($request->all())->save(). forceFill bypasses both $fillable and $guarded, and app/Models/Invoice.php:29 guards precisely account_id, total_cents, paid_at and credit_applied_cents - the fields this call makes writable.
findings.impact: A customer editing their own invoice can set total_cents to any value, stamp paid_at, apply credit, or reassign the row to another account_id, which is both financial fraud and a way to move records between tenants.
findings.recommendation: Validate an explicit field list and use fill() rather than forceFill(): $invoice->fill($request->validate(['status' => ..., 'due_at' => ..., 'notes' => ..., 'po_reference' => ...]))->save().

triage.reason: no form request, DTO or validate() call constrains the payload; forceFill is the documented way to defeat the model's own guard
total_cents, paid_at and account_id all carry security and financial impact, which is why the model guards them

findings.title: Application encryption key ships as a working literal default
findings.evidence: 'key' => env('APP_KEY', 'base64:[REDACTED:secret]') - a complete 32-byte base64 key committed as the fallback, with the comment above it stating the intent is that a fresh clone boots without key:generate. Sessions are configured encrypted (config/security.php:50), so this key protects the session payload as well as anything encrypt()ed.
findings.impact: Anyone with the repository can decrypt and forge encrypted cookies and any Crypt payload on any deployment where APP_KEY is not set in the environment - in practice session forgery and authentication bypass.
findings.recommendation: Remove the default so the framework fails to boot without APP_KEY, generate a fresh key per environment, and treat the committed value as compromised and rotated.

triage.reason: it is not a placeholder such as CHANGEME: it is a syntactically valid base64 AES-256 key that the framework will accept and use
the fallback is in the shipped configuration and applies whenever the environment variable is absent, which the surrounding comment presents as an expected state

findings.title: Debug mode defaults to on, including in production
findings.evidence: 'debug' => (bool) env('APP_DEBUG', true), directly under 'env' => env('APP_ENV', 'production'). The comment states the detailed handler 'stays on unless an operator explicitly turns it off', so the fail-open default is deliberate.
findings.impact: An unhandled exception returns the framework's detailed error page: file paths, framework and PHP versions, the failing SQL with bound values, and environment variables, which is also the easiest way to read back the results of the SQL injection above.
findings.recommendation: Default to false - env('APP_DEBUG', false) - and return a generic error with a correlation id, keeping the detail in the server log.

triage.reason: the default is evaluated in the shipped config and the sibling key on line 15 defaults APP_ENV to production, so the debug path is the production path when the variable is unset
no exception handler in the tree replaces the framework page

findings.title: CORS allows every origin while carrying credentials
findings.evidence: 'allowed_origins' => ['*'] at line 28 together with 'supports_credentials' => true at line 38. The comment above explains the intent is to echo whatever the browser sends so new tenant vanity domains keep working; with credentials enabled the CORS middleware cannot emit a literal '*' and reflects the requesting Origin instead, which is origin reflection.
findings.impact: Any web page a portal user visits can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the paths covered by this policy and read the responses, turning any site into an authenticated reader of the customer's billing data.
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with the tenant domains resolved at request time from the database, comparing the full origin string, and keep supports_credentials only for that exact list.

triage.reason: no other layer in the tree restricts Origin; the paths key on line 19 limits which URLs the policy attaches to, not which origins it trusts
the responses behind these paths are per-customer invoice data
the comment shows the wildcard is a convenience to avoid a redeploy, not a bounded public surface

findings.title: Session cookie is readable by scripts, allowed over plain HTTP and sent cross-site
findings.evidence: 'http_only' => false at line 62, 'secure' => false at line 68 and 'same_site' => 'none' at line 70, each with a comment describing live behaviour: the embedded PDF viewer reads the session id out of document.cookie, and the edge load balancer is expected to redirect :80 to https.
findings.impact: Any script on the page - or injected into it - can read the session id and no browser rule stops the cookie from riding a plaintext request; SameSite=None removes the last cross-site restriction, so the cookie is attached to requests from any origin.
findings.recommendation: Set http_only and secure to true and same_site to 'lax'; give the PDF worker a short-lived scoped token issued server-side instead of letting a script read the session cookie.

triage.reason: an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect at the edge does not protect the first plaintext request that already carries the cookie, and nothing else re-adds HttpOnly
this is the only session configuration in the tree and its comments describe production components, not a development shortcut

findings.title: Declared password policy is enforced nowhere
findings.evidence: The config declares min_length 12, require_mixed_case true and check_compromised true (lines 84-88). Grepping the tree for a reader of config('security...') returns nothing, and the only password-setting path validates ['required','string','min:12','confirmed'] (AuthController.php:81) - the length is duplicated by hand, the other two requirements have no implementation anywhere.
findings.impact: Users can set a lower-case-only password and one already in a breach corpus, while the configuration and any review of it say otherwise; a declared control that nothing reads is worse than an absent one because the project believes it holds it.
findings.recommendation: Enforce the three requirements in one place - a Password rule chain with mixedCase() and uncompromised() driven by these config keys - or delete the keys so the configuration stops asserting a control that does not exist.
findings.unaided_label: billing password policy declared not enforced

triage.reason: a service provider outside this tree could merge config/security.php and register the rules; nothing in the given files does, and App\Providers\AppServiceProvider is referenced in config/app.php:72 but not supplied. What would settle it: the AppServiceProvider and the auth service provider sources
the keys are plain scalars, not an env-tagged struct read wholesale, so a symbol search is a valid way to look for the reader

findings.title: Password reset leaves every existing session valid
findings.evidence: resetPassword forceFills the new hash and marks the reset row used (lines 93-94), then redirects. No call to Auth::logoutOtherDevices, no session invalidation, no rehash of the remember token - compare logout() at line 47, which does invalidate and regenerate.
findings.impact: The user whose account was taken over resets their password and the attacker's session keeps working, which is the failure mode a password reset exists to fix.
findings.recommendation: After saving the new hash, invalidate the user's other sessions and rotate the remember token.
findings.unaided_label: billing reset does not kill sessions

triage.reason: the session driver is redis (config/security.php:44) with an 8-hour lifetime and expire_on_close false, so nothing expires the old session on a credential change
there is no server-side equivalent elsewhere; the sessions simply survive

findings.title: Login lockout is keyed to the IP only, with no per-account limit
findings.evidence: ->middleware('throttle:5,1') on POST /login. The unnamed throttle middleware keys on the request IP, not on the submitted identity; the comment beside it claims 'per ip+email' and adds that this is the only lockout the portal has. Nothing in AuthController::login counts failures against the account.
findings.impact: Credential stuffing distributed across addresses is unlimited against any single account, and a targeted account never locks; the audit line at line 32 records the attempts but nothing acts on them.
findings.recommendation: Add a named RateLimiter keyed on the lower-cased email as well as the IP, and lock the account after a threshold with an unlock path.

triage.reason: the throttle middleware is the only limiter on the route and its key is the IP; no second layer counts per identity

findings.title: JWT signature validation is replaced by a parser that verifies nothing
findings.evidence: SignatureValidator = (token, _) => new JwtSecurityToken(token). The delegate constructs the token from the string and returns it; it performs no cryptographic check, and supplying a SignatureValidator suppresses the library's own signature verification. IssuerSigningKey is built on line 19 and then never used for anything. The comment attributes the change to JWKS latency at cold start.
findings.impact: Anyone can mint a token with the expected iss and aud and any claims they like - role=fleet-admin, any tenant_id - and the API accepts it. Every route behind the fallback authorization policy, including firmware promotion, is open to an unauthenticated attacker.
findings.recommendation: Delete the SignatureValidator override and let the handler verify against the IssuerSigningKey, or wire a cached IssuerSigningKeyResolver over JWKS with a background refresh; never trade signature verification for a cold-start second.

triage.reason: the issuer and audience checks the comment leans on are string comparisons against values printed inside the token itself; there is no layer that verifies the token was signed by anyone
the returned JwtSecurityToken becomes the ClaimsPrincipal for the request, so its claims govern authorization - see DevicesController.cs:22 and the fleet-admin policy at Program.cs:35
the delegate is in the single code path that builds validation parameters for the JwtBearer handler registered at Program.cs:24

findings.title: SQL injection in the device serial search
findings.evidence: FromSqlRaw($"SELECT TOP 25 * FROM devices WHERE tenant_id = {TenantId} AND serial LIKE '%{q}%' ORDER BY serial"). FromSqlRaw takes a string, so the C# interpolation is performed before the call and nothing is parameterised - unlike FromSqlInterpolated, which would turn the same syntax into bound parameters. q is the raw query-string value.
findings.impact: An attacker closes the literal and appends arbitrary T-SQL under the API's database identity, reading or modifying every tenant's devices; the tenant_id predicate on the same line is injected text and is bypassed with it.
findings.recommendation: Switch to FromSqlInterpolated with the identical string, or pass parameters explicitly: FromSqlRaw("... serial LIKE {0} ...", "%" + q + "%").

triage.reason: q is [FromQuery] string with only a null/whitespace check at line 47
no allowlist or escaping stands between the query string and the statement

findings.title: Device retirement is explicitly anonymous and unscoped
findings.evidence: [AllowAnonymous] on HttpDelete("{id:long}"), the only opt-out from the fallback policy declared at Program.cs:31. The body then loads the device by primary key alone - FirstOrDefaultAsync(d => d.Id == id) - with no TenantId predicate, unlike List at line 31 and Stats at line 68 which both filter on TenantId. The comment attributes the exemption to the console calling before the SSO hop completes.
findings.impact: Anyone on the network can retire any device in any tenant by walking numeric ids: a one-request denial of service against a whole fleet, with the affected serials written to the log as the only trace.
findings.recommendation: Remove [AllowAnonymous], scope the lookup with TenantId as the sibling actions do, and give the console a pre-SSO token rather than an open endpoint.

triage.reason: the fallback policy at Program.cs:31 is the mandatory layer and this attribute is precisely the documented way to skip it
the second principal is any other tenant, and the third is any unauthenticated caller
the exposure is a workaround for a login race, not a bounded public surface: the endpoint mutates state

findings.title: Production database password committed in appsettings.Production.json and copied to build output
findings.evidence: "Server=sql-fleet-prod.internal,1433;Database=Fleet;User Id=fleet_app;Password=[REDACTED:secret];...". The project deliberately propagates the file: FleetApi.csproj:24 declares <None Update="appsettings.Production.json"><CopyToOutputDirectory>PreserveNewest, so it lands in every build output including developer machines. The project also declares a UserSecretsId (csproj:8), which is the mechanism this credential should have used.
findings.impact: Every holder of the repository or of any build artifact has the production database credential and the internal host and port to use it against.
findings.recommendation: Move the connection string to the environment or the secret store already referenced by UserSecretsId, drop the CopyToOutputDirectory entry, rotate the password, and treat the committed value as disclosed.

triage.reason: it is a concrete password against a named production host, not a placeholder or a documented test value
the csproj explicitly copies this file into the shipped output

findings.title: Token expiry is disabled in production and the clock skew is a day
findings.evidence: "ValidateLifetime": false and "ClockSkewMinutes": 1440 in the production file, overriding the development values of true and 2 (appsettings.json:15-16). TokenService.cs:29-30 reads both keys. The note attributes it to field gateways replaying buffered telemetry with a stale token.
findings.impact: A token that leaks once is valid forever: revocation by expiry does not exist, and the 24-hour skew would still accept a day-old token even if lifetime validation were re-enabled.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable ValidateLifetime with a small skew and solve the offline-replay case in the telemetry protocol - sign the batch at upload time, or accept buffered data on a separate endpoint that authenticates the gateway rather than the payload's age.

triage.reason: the setting is in the production configuration file, which is the environment it names
there is no revocation list or introspection call anywhere in the tree to compensate; the jti minted at TokenService.cs:49 is never checked against a store

findings.title: Production MQTT broker is reached in plaintext with TLS explicitly disabled
findings.evidence: "BrokerUri": "tcp://mqtt-fleet-prod.internal:1883" with "TlsRequired": false and a "Username": "fleet-api", against the development file's "tls://broker.localhost:8883" with TlsRequired true. The note says the broker shares a VPC subnet and the gateways cannot be re-flashed with the CA bundle. MQTTnet.AspNetCore is referenced at FleetApi.csproj:18.
findings.impact: Telemetry and the broker credential travel unencrypted and unauthenticated on the wire; anyone with a position on that subnet can read fleet telemetry and publish commands as the API.
findings.recommendation: Terminate TLS on the broker and pin the internal CA in the API; run the un-flashed gateways through a bridge that upgrades the hop rather than turning TLS off for everyone.

triage.reason: a shared VPC subnet is not an authenticated channel, and the note itself frames the setting as a temporary accommodation

no file in the given tree reads the Mqtt section, so I cannot show the connection is made from this code; the MQTTnet.AspNetCore package reference is the only evidence the client exists. What would settle it: the MQTT client registration and its use of Mqtt:TlsRequired

findings.title: Administrative privilege is granted by a request header
findings.evidence: let elevated = headers.get("X-Flags-Elevate") ... eq_ignore_ascii_case("true"), then is_admin: elevated || data.claims.roles.iter().any(|r| r == admin_claim) at line 59. The header is read from the same HeaderMap as the bearer token and is not covered by the token signature. routes.rs:112 and :138 are the only authorization checks in the service and both consult is_admin.
findings.impact: Any caller holding any valid token for any tenant adds one header and becomes an administrator: create, overwrite and archive flags, and set the webhook URL that the service then fetches server-side.
findings.recommendation: Delete the header path. If on-call engineers need elevation, mint a short-lived token carrying the admin claim from the console's own credentials so the privilege is inside the signature. If an ingress is expected to strip X-Flags-Elevate before it reaches the service, that stripping is not visible in this tree and would in any case leave the privilege decision outside the token.

triage.reason: nothing between the client and this function strips or validates X-Flags-Elevate; the console is described as a proxy, not as the only reachable path
the value is a raw request header, fully attacker-controlled

findings.title: SQL injection in the flag search term
findings.evidence: The statement is assembled with format! and the search term is captured inline: "AND (key ILIKE '%{term}%' OR description ILIKE '%{term}%')". tenant_id on the line above is a bound $1 parameter, so the same call proves binding was available. term is ListQuery.q, deserialized straight from the query string (routes.rs:23, :57).
findings.impact: Any token holder reads or writes every tenant's flags, and because handler errors are returned verbatim to the client (routes.rs:59) the injection is error-based and needs no blind technique.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term as a parameter: keep the ORDER BY fragment from the enums and pass '%'||$2||'%' to ILIKE.

triage.reason: q is a serde-defaulted String taken from the query string with no validation
sqlx's compile-time checking is not in play here: query_as with a runtime &str skips it, and no escaping is applied

findings.title: Server-side request forgery through the flag's webhook URL
findings.evidence: state.http.post(url) where url is flag.webhook_url, stored verbatim from the FlagUpsert body (model.rs:72, store.rs:74) and fired whenever rollout_percent reaches 100 (routes.rs:124). There is no scheme check, no host allowlist, no address resolution check, and the reqwest client is built at main.rs:85 with only a timeout - redirect following is left at its default.
findings.impact: A caller who can upsert a flag makes the service issue POSTs from inside the deployment network: cloud metadata endpoints, other services on the VPC, or loopback administrative ports, with the JSON body under the caller's control. The response status is reflected back at routes.rs:128, giving a coarse read channel.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the host before connecting and reject loopback, link-local and private ranges; require https; disable redirect following; and keep an owner-approved destination allowlist as the primary control.

triage.reason: the only gate before the fetch is the is_admin check at routes.rs:112, which the header at auth.rs:50 hands to any token holder; nothing validates the URL itself
webhook_url comes from the request body and is persisted unchanged
the outbound call is unbounded rather than confined to a declared integration surface

findings.title: Webhook signature falls back to an empty HMAC key when the environment variable is unset
findings.evidence: let secret = std::env::var("FLAGS_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_KEY").unwrap_or_default(); followed by HmacSha256::new_from_slice(secret.as_bytes()).expect("hmac accepts any key size"). The expect message states the design assumption that makes the failure silent: HMAC accepts a zero-length key, so a missing variable produces a well-formed signature over a publicly known key. The variable appears nowhere else in the tree - not in docker-compose.yml, not in config/default.toml.
findings.impact: Every receiver that verifies X-Flags-Signature accepts forged notifications, because anyone can compute HMAC-SHA256 with an empty key; the control reports success while providing no authenticity at all.
findings.recommendation: Read the key at start-up into AppState and refuse to boot when it is absent or shorter than 32 bytes, so a missing secret is a deployment failure rather than a silent downgrade.

triage.reason: there is no start-up validation of the variable anywhere in main.rs, and no other signature is applied to the request
the fallback is in the shipped signing path, and no file in the tree sets the variable
there is no second authenticity mechanism on the callback; this signature is the whole control

findings.title: The Docker socket is mounted into the application container
findings.evidence: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock on the api service, the same service that publishes 8080 to the host and terminates untrusted HTTP. The comment says the rollout job shells out to docker restart on sidecar workers.
findings.impact: Access to the socket is equivalent to root on the host: any code execution inside the API container - and this service has a SQL injection and an SSRF - becomes full host compromise, escaping every container boundary on the machine.
findings.recommendation: Remove the mount. Have the rollout publish a message that a small privileged helper consumes, or use the orchestrator's own restart API with a scoped credential; never give an internet-facing process the daemon socket.

triage.reason: this is not a system container such as a CNI or node agent: it is the public API service, and the socket serves a convenience restart
no rootless builder, socket proxy or capability restriction is declared anywhere in the file

findings.title: Database password in the compose environment while a docker secret is declared beside it
findings.evidence: FLAGS__DATABASE__URL: postgres://flags:[REDACTED:secret]@db:5432/flags at line 11 and repeated for the migrate service at line 46, while the db service on the same file takes POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE from a declared docker secret (lines 31-33, 52-54). The correct mechanism is present in the file and is not used by the two consumers.
findings.impact: The database password is in the repository and in every environment listing of the running container (docker inspect, /proc/<pid>/environ), so it leaks to anyone who can read the tree or the host.
findings.recommendation: Give api and migrate the same secret the db service uses and assemble the URL from the mounted file at start-up, keeping the credential out of both the repository and the process environment.

triage.reason: it is a real password shaped like a service credential, not a placeholder, and it is what the two services actually connect with
the file is the deployment descriptor for the tagged image registry.internal/edge-flags:0.6.2

findings.title: Database and token-validation error text is returned to the caller
findings.evidence: Every handler maps its error with (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, e.to_string()) - lines 59, 73, 78, 93, 100, 122, 144, 149 - and the tuple's String becomes the response body. AuthError::Rejected(m) at line 46 does the same for the JWT library's own message.
findings.impact: Callers read raw Postgres errors, including the failing statement text and column names, which turns the SQL injection above into a directly readable channel, and read the token library's reason for rejection, which helps shape a forged token.
findings.recommendation: Log the error with a correlation id and return a fixed message; keep the detail server-side.
findings.unaided_label: edge sqlx error text to client

triage.reason: no error-mapping middleware sits above the router; the tuple is serialised straight into the response by axum's IntoResponse
the text carries internal schema and statement fragments, not public content

findings.title: The decoding key is built from the issuer URL, so token verification can never succeed
findings.evidence: DecodingKey::from_rsa_pem(state.settings.auth.issuer.as_bytes()) - the value passed as PEM is the issuer string, which config/default.toml:16 sets to "https://id.internal.example/realms/platform" and which is passed again as the issuer on line 40. from_rsa_pem cannot parse that, so the map_err on line 35 fires and every authenticated request returns 500. The comment claims the realm's public key is fetched at boot and cached alongside the pool; AppState (main.rs:60) holds only the pool, the settings and an http client - there is no cached key.
findings.impact: Every route under /api/v1 answers 500: a total outage of the service's functional surface. It also means the signature-verification path has never run, so no evidence exists that the JWT configuration works, and the obvious fix under outage pressure is to weaken the check.
findings.recommendation: Fetch the JWKS at start-up, store the DecodingKey in AppState, and add a test that a token signed by the wrong key is rejected - a negative test, so the control cannot pass by never running.
findings.unaided_label: edge decoding key from issuer url

triage.reason: this finding is that a control is inoperative, not that one is missing; it fails closed, which is why the impact is availability rather than bypass
there is no reading under which an https URL string is an RSA PEM; the same field is used as the issuer four lines later

findings.title: Configured request, statement and body limits have no enforcement anywhere
findings.evidence: config/default.toml declares server.request_timeout_ms, server.shutdown_grace_ms, database.statement_timeout_ms, webhooks.max_body_bytes, evaluation.max_rules_per_flag, evaluation.max_variants and evaluation.default_ttl_seconds. Grepping src/ for each name returns only the struct field declarations in main.rs (lines 20, 21, 28, 47) and nothing at all for the three evaluation keys. No TimeoutLayer is added to the router even though tower-http's timeout feature is enabled (Cargo.toml:12), the pool at main.rs:80 sets only max_connections, and no body-size layer is registered. The one limit that is enforced, webhooks.timeout_ms at main.rs:86, shows what a consumed key looks like.
findings.impact: A slow or expensive request is never cut off and a slow query is never cancelled, so an unauthenticated flood or a single pathological statement can pin connections until the pool is exhausted; an operator tuning these knobs changes nothing, which is the more expensive half - the deployment believes it has limits.
findings.recommendation: Apply the values: a tower-http TimeoutLayer from request_timeout_ms, SET statement_timeout on connection from statement_timeout_ms, DefaultBodyLimit from max_body_bytes, and a graceful-shutdown future from shutdown_grace_ms; delete the evaluation keys or implement them.

triage.reason: the values are read into a plain deserialized struct that is consumed by symbol, so a symbol search is a valid way to count readers - and one sibling key, webhooks.timeout_ms, is found that way at main.rs:86

an ingress could impose a body size or timeout in front of the service, but no such artifact is in the tree; docker-compose.yml publishes the port directly. What would settle it: the ingress or reverse-proxy configuration for this deployment

findings.title: The session cookie is unsigned base64 JSON that the client can write
findings.evidence: readSession base64url-decodes the cookie, JSON.parses it and returns userId, workspaceId and role straight from the payload; the only checks are presence and an issuedAt age. writeSession (line 50) is its exact inverse with no MAC or encryption. The file's own comment says the cookie is httpOnly so page scripts never touch it - which is not a property that stops a client from crafting the value. crypto is imported but used only by the unreferenced verifyLegacySession.
findings.impact: Anyone sets nw_session to base64url of {"userId":"...","workspaceId":"<victim>","role":"admin","issuedAt":<now>} and is that user in that workspace, with admin role, everywhere the app reads the session: the middleware gate (middleware.ts:27) and every server action (app/actions/notes.ts:22). It is full authentication and tenant bypass with no credential.
findings.recommendation: Sign or encrypt the cookie with a server key and verify before trusting it, or switch to an opaque identifier resolved against a server-side session store; reject the cookie when verification fails.

triage.reason: every consumer in the tree calls readSession and no layer verifies integrity: middleware.ts:27 and app/actions/notes.ts:22 are the two call sites
the parsed object is the authorization subject - role is read at line 41 and workspaceId scopes the note queries at actions/notes.ts:35 and :46

findings.title: The middleware reflects any Origin and allows credentials
findings.evidence: res.headers.set('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', origin) where origin is req.headers.get('origin'), immediately followed by Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: 'true'. There is no comparison against any list; the comment says the desktop app, the extension and the marketing site each need the cookie to ride along, so 'hand back whichever origin asked'.
findings.impact: Any site a signed-in user visits can read authenticated responses from this workspace with the user's cookie attached, which is a cross-origin read of every note the user can see.
findings.recommendation: Compare the Origin against a closed list and echo it only on a match; drop Allow-Credentials for anything outside that list.

triage.reason: this middleware is the only place CORS headers are set in the tree; next.config.mjs:20 adds three unrelated headers
the responses are the user's private notes
the header is set on the response for every matched path, before the authentication branch, so it applies to authenticated responses too

findings.title: The share endpoint requires no session and never checks note ownership
findings.evidence: The handler reads noteId, validates the destination, fetches the note with getNote(body.noteId) and posts its title and rendered html upstream. readSession is called at line 36 but only to attribute the audit row - session?.userId ?? 'unknown' at line 49 - and its result is never branched on. The route is also outside the middleware gate: the matcher at middleware.ts:45 excludes api, so nothing else authenticates it.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller who knows or guesses a note id pushes that note's full contents to one of the three configured integration hosts, exfiltrating private notes from any workspace with no credential at all; the share is recorded as 'unknown'.
findings.recommendation: Require a valid session at the top of the handler and return 401 without one, then verify the note's workspace_id matches the session's workspace before fetching or forwarding it.

triage.reason: the matcher at middleware.ts:45 explicitly excludes api from the gate, and the handler's own readSession call is not consulted for a decision - the WEB-27 shape, a control that runs and cannot fail
the second principal is every other workspace, and the caller need not be a principal at all
the forwarded body is the note's title and rendered content

findings.title: Note update authenticates the caller but never checks the note is theirs
findings.evidence: currentSession() is called for its throw and its return value is discarded - note the bare currentSession(); on line 58 against const session = currentSession(); in the two sibling actions. getNote(input.id!) then loads any note by uuid and saveNote overwrites it. createNoteAction at line 46 passes session.workspaceId and session.userId; lib/db.ts:46 scopes the UPDATE by id alone.
findings.impact: Any signed-in user - and, given the forgeable cookie, anyone - overwrites the title and body of any note in any workspace by supplying its id.
findings.recommendation: Compare the loaded note's workspace_id (and owner where the product requires it) against the session before saving, or scope the UPDATE itself: WHERE id = $1 AND workspace_id = $2.

triage.reason: the mandatory layer here is the server action itself; middleware.ts does not see server-action targets by object id, and lib/db.ts applies no scope
notes are workspace-private: every other query in the file filters by workspaceId

findings.title: The note page renders any note id without a workspace check
findings.evidence: const note = await getNote(params.id) with no session read and no workspace comparison; lib/db.ts:20 selects by id alone. generateMetadata at line 10 does the same, so even the page title leaks. The middleware ahead of it (middleware.ts:27) establishes only that some session cookie decodes, never that the note belongs to it.
findings.impact: Any user with a session - forgeable per the cookie finding - reads any note in any workspace by id, including its rendered body.
findings.recommendation: Read the session in the page, pass workspaceId into the query, and return notFound() when the note is outside it.

triage.reason: the middleware is an authentication gate, not an object-level one; it cannot know which note the id names
the path is not in PUBLIC_PREFIXES (middleware.ts:5), so the product treats notes as private
ids are uuids, which raises the cost of guessing but is not an access control - and the share endpoint above accepts the same ids from an unauthenticated caller

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy on a page that injects stored HTML
findings.evidence: The headers() block sets X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and X-Frame-Options and no Content-Security-Policy, while app/notes/[id]/page.tsx:33 renders stored note.html through dangerouslySetInnerHTML. The markdown renderer's escaping (lib/policy.ts:34) is the only thing standing between a note author and script execution.
findings.impact: The escaping control is load-bearing and alone: any future change to the renderer options, a markdown-it parsing bug, or another writer into the html column becomes immediate script execution with no second layer to reduce it - and the session cookie is read by the middleware rather than being unreadable to script.
findings.recommendation: Add a CSP with a nonce and no unsafe-inline to the same headers() block, so the sanitiser is defence in depth rather than the whole defence.

triage.reason: FP-10 downgrades rather than deletes, and this is already reported at the floor severity: the renderer control works today, so the impact is the absence of a second layer, which is exactly what is written here

a CDN could add the header; nothing in the tree does, and the presence of a curated headers() block is evidence this is where the project sets them. What would settle it: the edge or CDN header configuration

findings.title: A client cookie is deserialized with pickle
findings.evidence: saved = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(raw_cookie)) where raw_cookie = request.COOKIES.get("hd_filters") on line 48. The try/except on line 53 catches the exception after the fact - pickle executes during reconstruction, so the guard runs too late to matter. Nothing signs or verifies the cookie.
findings.impact: Remote code execution on the web server as the application user by anyone who can set a cookie and reach /tickets/ - which, given the login gate, means any help desk user, and pivots to the database credentials, the attachment volume and the Celery broker.
findings.recommendation: Store the layout as JSON and json.loads it, or sign the value with django.core.signing; never unpickle anything that crossed the network.

triage.reason: the value is a request cookie, entirely under the client's control
pickle reconstructs arbitrary objects and invokes __reduce__ during load; it is the canonical executing sink
no signature is verified before the load; the except clause runs after execution

findings.title: Command injection through the export filename
findings.evidence: subprocess.run(f"zip -j -q {dest} {tmp_path}", shell=True, check=True) where dest = os.path.join(settings.EXPORT_ROOT, filename + ".zip") on line 40 and filename arrives from request.GET.get("filename", ...) at views.py:96 and is queued unvalidated at views.py:98. The docstring states the agent names the file, so the value is meant to be client-chosen. The neighbouring task at line 59 shows the safe shape - a path built from a uuid and an allowlisted extension.
findings.impact: Any authenticated help desk user gets arbitrary shell execution on the Celery worker by putting a shell metacharacter in the filename; the same value also traverses out of EXPORT_ROOT via ../. The worker holds the database credentials and the attachment volume.
findings.recommendation: Drop shell=True and pass an argument list, and derive the on-disk name server-side (a uuid) while keeping the agent's label only as the download's Content-Disposition filename.

triage.reason: traced backwards, the value is the filename query parameter with no validation between views.py:96 and the f-string
no allowlist, quoting or shlex call is applied on either side of the queue boundary
the string form with shell=True is a real shell, not an argv list

findings.title: Django SECRET_KEY has a committed fallback
findings.evidence: SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get("DJANGO_SECRET_KEY", "django-insecure-hd-[REDACTED:secret]") - a complete usable key as the default, so any deployment that does not set the variable runs on the value in the repository.
findings.impact: The key signs session cookies, CSRF tokens, password-reset tokens and anything through django.core.signing. Knowing it means forging a session for any user, including staff, and defeating CSRF - which pairs directly with the unconditional admin delete permission below.
findings.recommendation: Read the key with os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"] so a missing value stops the boot, rotate the current one, and treat sessions signed with it as compromised.

triage.reason: the string is a working key, not a placeholder: Django accepts it and will sign with it
it is the shipped default in the only settings module, applying whenever the environment variable is absent

findings.title: DEBUG defaults to on
findings.evidence: DEBUG = os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG", "1") == "1" - the default is the debug state, and the comment above says agents paste the yellow error page into escalation tickets, which is how the rules get debugged.
findings.impact: Any unhandled exception returns Django's technical 500 page: the settings dump with database credentials and SECRET_KEY partially rendered, the full traceback, local variables and the SQL executed. Copying that page into a ticket also spreads it to whoever reads the ticket.
findings.recommendation: Default the variable to off, and give agents a correlation id plus a server-side log lookup instead of the debug page.

triage.reason: the default lives in the settings module the WSGI application loads (settings.py:81), and no production settings module overrides it in this tree
no custom 500 handler exists in config/urls.py to intercept the response

findings.title: Open redirect after sign-in
findings.evidence: return redirect(request.GET.get("next", settings.LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL)) with no validation. Django's own LoginView guards the same parameter with url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme; this hand-rolled view does not, and the middleware that produces the parameter (tickets/middleware.py:18) is not the only way it can be set - the attacker supplies it directly.
findings.impact: A link to the real help desk sign-in URL lands the user on an attacker's page immediately after a successful authentication, which is the strongest moment for a credential-replay or consent phishing prompt.
findings.recommendation: Validate the target with django.utils.http.url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme against request.get_host() and fall back to LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL when it fails.

triage.reason: no allowlist or host check runs anywhere on this path; the value goes straight into redirect()
next is a query-string parameter and the attacker chooses the whole URL, including scheme and host

findings.title: Session and CSRF cookies are permitted over plain HTTP
findings.evidence: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = False, with the comment stating TLS terminates at the branch office proxy and the last hop to the app servers is plain http. No SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT and no SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS are set anywhere in the module, so nothing pushes the browser back to https either.
findings.impact: The session and CSRF cookies are sent in the clear on the internal hop and on any accidental http request, so anyone positioned on that network reads them and takes over the session.
findings.recommendation: Set both to True and terminate TLS on the app servers, or run the last hop over a mutually authenticated tunnel; add SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT and HSTS.

triage.reason: the cleartext hop is an internal network, which is not a bounded intended exposure for a session cookie - it is exactly the position an attacker wants
this is the only settings module in the tree and it is the one WSGI_APPLICATION loads

findings.title: Admin delete permission is granted unconditionally
findings.evidence: def has_delete_permission(self, request, obj=None): return True on the base class inherited by QueueAdmin, TicketAdmin, CommentAdmin and AttachmentAdmin. It overrides Django's model-permission check with a constant, and the sibling OrganizationAdmin at line 33 shows the intended shape: return request.user.is_superuser. It is the WEB-27 pattern - a permission hook that runs and has no arm that says no.
findings.impact: Any staff user who can open the admin can delete queues, tickets, comments and attachments in their organization regardless of the delete permissions assigned to them, so the permission grid in the admin no longer describes what users can do. Ticket and attachment deletion also destroys the audit trail.
findings.recommendation: Delete the override and let Django evaluate the model permission, or return a real decision such as request.user.has_perm(...) combined with the org scope.

triage.reason: get_queryset (line 16) bounds which rows are visible, not whether the user may delete them; the two are different axes and only the first is enforced
there is no server-side equivalent elsewhere - this method is the delete decision
it is not a base-class default that subclasses override: all four registered subclasses inherit it unchanged

findings.title: SECURITY DEFINER function runs with a caller-controlled search_path
findings.evidence: post_journal is declared LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER and owned by ledger_owner (line 111), with no SET search_path clause - unlike ledger.current_tenant (002_rls.sql:24), ledger.archive_account (line 84) and even ledger.account_balance_at (line 9), which all pin one. Its body then references journals, entries and audit_log unqualified (lines 56, 60, 68), so those names resolve through the caller's search_path, and pg_temp is searched ahead of the schema list.
findings.impact: ledger_app - the role the API connects as - creates temporary tables named journals, entries and audit_log, calls post_journal, and the definer-context inserts land in objects the caller owns. With a trigger or a default expression on those objects the caller executes arbitrary SQL as ledger_owner, which owns the schema, so it is a full escalation out of the RLS model that the rest of this directory is built on.
findings.recommendation: Add SET search_path = ledger, pg_temp to post_journal, exactly as its two siblings do, and schema-qualify the three INSERT targets; make the clause a review requirement for every SECURITY DEFINER routine.

triage.reason: REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC (004_grants.sql:32) removes one hiding place but not pg_temp, which every role may create in and which is resolved first for unqualified table names
the two principals are explicit in the file: ledger_app, a LOGIN role granted EXECUTE at 004_grants.sql:27, and ledger_owner, the schema owner the function runs as
the three sibling routines in the same directory carry the clause, so its absence here is a difference and not a house style

findings.title: Provisioning downloads migrations over plain HTTP and applies them as the schema owner
findings.evidence: MIGRATION_MIRROR="http://artifacts.internal.example/ledger/migrations" (line 17), curl -fsSL "${MIGRATION_MIRROR}/${ENVIRONMENT}/latest.tar.gz" (line 48), tar -xzf into STAGE_DIR (line 49) with no signature check, no checksum and no member-path validation, and then every *.sql in that directory is executed with psql -U ledger_owner (lines 82-86).
findings.impact: Anyone able to answer for that hostname or sit on the path - plain HTTP, so no certificate is involved - ships SQL that runs as the schema owner on the ledger database: arbitrary schema and data changes, new roles, or a definer function left behind as a backdoor. The tar extraction adds a path-traversal write outside STAGE_DIR on top.
findings.recommendation: Fetch over https, verify a detached signature or a pinned checksum before extraction, extract with member-path validation, and apply the staged files only after verification fails closed.

triage.reason: the payload is remote content over an unauthenticated channel; ENVIRONMENT is a script argument that also selects the path
set -euo pipefail and ON_ERROR_STOP make the script fail on error, which is not integrity; nothing verifies what was downloaded
an internal mirror is a host on a network, not an authenticated source: the comment describes it as the release engineers' publishing point, which is the thing to authenticate

findings.title: The database credential file is written world-readable
findings.evidence: chmod 0644 "${CONFIG_DIR}/db.env" on a file the script has just written containing LEDGER_DB_PASSWORD=${APP_PASSWORD} (lines 59-65). The comment gives the reason - the API container, the reporting sidecar and the on-call shell all source it and do not share a group. backup.sh:14 sources the same file. The script demonstrates it knows better twenty lines later: the pooler userlist is written under umask 0177 and chowned to a service account (lines 101-107).
findings.impact: Every local account on the host, including any compromised unprivileged service, reads the ledger_app password and connects to the ledger directly, which is under the RLS model the only thing standing between a process and every tenant's journals.
findings.recommendation: Create a shared group for the three consumers and write the file 0640 root:that-group, or hand each consumer its own credential from the secret store rather than a shared readable file.

triage.reason: the second principal is every other local account on the host; the comment names three distinct consumers with no common group, which is the boundary
the file's content is a live production database password

findings.title: The shared export directory is made world-writable
findings.evidence: chmod -R 0777 "$EXPORT_DIR" (/srv/ledger/exports), justified by the comment that the API writes statement bundles there and the reporting sidecar, the nightly archiver and the ops jobs pick them up under their own accounts. No sticky bit is set, and -R applies it to existing content as well as the directory.
findings.impact: Any local account reads every customer statement bundle in the directory and, because write is granted without the sticky bit, replaces or deletes another process's file - so a downstream job can be fed a substituted statement.
findings.recommendation: Use a shared group with 2770 and setgid so files inherit it, or hand off through an object store with per-consumer credentials.

triage.reason: the boundary is between the four named service accounts and every other local account, which 0777 erases
the directory holds financial statement bundles per tenant
the intended sharing is between four known accounts; 0777 is not a bound on that set

findings.title: Role passwords are passed on the psql command line
findings.evidence: psql ... -c "ALTER ROLE ledger_app PASSWORD '${APP_PASSWORD}'" -c "ALTER ROLE ledger_report PASSWORD '${REPORT_PASSWORD}'". The script already knows the safer channel: the owner password on line 75 travels through PGPASSWORD in the environment rather than argv.
findings.impact: Both passwords are visible in the host process table for the life of the command to every local user, and the statement text is written verbatim to the Postgres server log whenever statement logging is on - a durable copy of a live credential in a file with different readers.
findings.recommendation: Feed the statements to psql on stdin with a here-document, and use \password or a SCRAM verifier computed client-side so the cleartext never appears in argv or in the server log.

triage.reason: argv is readable by other local accounts, and the database log has its own readership
no other mechanism removes the credential from argv; the window is short but the log copy is not

findings.title: Transaction pooling undermines the session setting that row-level security depends on
findings.evidence: pool_mode = transaction with server_reset_query = DISCARD ALL. Every policy in 002_rls.sql resolves through ledger.current_tenant(), which reads current_setting('app.tenant_id') - a session-scoped GUC. The two files disagree about when it is set: 002_rls.sql:3 says every connection sets it 'right after checkout (see the pool's on-connect hook)', while pgbouncer.ini:17 says the app re-applies it on checkout because a connection can be handed over at a transaction boundary. Under transaction pooling a server connection is reassigned per transaction and the reset query is not run between transactions by default, so a value set once per connection outlives the client that set it.
findings.impact: A transaction that does not set app.tenant_id itself inherits the previous client's value, and every RLS policy then evaluates against the wrong tenant - cross-tenant reads and writes of accounts, journals and entries, with the audit rows attributed to the wrong tenant too. It fails open rather than closed: an unset GUC yields NULL and returns nothing, but a stale one returns another tenant's rows.
findings.recommendation: Set app.tenant_id with SET LOCAL inside each transaction, never on connect; add server_reset_query_always = 1 as a backstop; and assert at the start of each transaction that the GUC matches the authenticated tenant.
findings.unaided_label: ledger pgbouncer transaction pooling vs RLS GUC

triage.reason: RLS is the mandatory layer, but its predicate is a session variable the pooler does not scope; the policies cannot compensate for being fed a stale tenant

the application's connection code is outside this tree, so I cannot show whether it uses SET or SET LOCAL; the in-tree evidence is the contradiction between 002_rls.sql:3, which describes a per-connection hook, and pgbouncer.ini:17-18. What would settle it: the API's pool checkout code, or a pgbouncer.ini carrying server_reset_query_always = 1
